claim_verdicts.evidence: servers/index.md: "Kestrel server is the default, cross-platform HTTP server implementation." kestrel.md (moniker >= aspnetcore-10.0): "Kestrel is the recommended server for ASP.NET Core, and it's configured by default in ASP.NET Core project templates."

servers/index.md: "An ASP.NET Core app runs with an in-process HTTP server implementation. The server implementation listens for HTTP requests and surfaces them to the app as a set of request features composed into an HttpContext." 'request object' is an acceptable L1 simplification; TCP is scoped to HTTP/1.1 in the lesson text.

servers/index.md: "the request is pushed into the ASP.NET Core middleware pipeline. The middleware pipeline handles the request and passes it on as an HttpContext instance to the app's logic." Routing and app logic sit after the server, not in it.

Caddyfile@stage-0 (commit ff911b0) L14-17: @postOrder = method POST, path /api/v1/orders; L36-39: header Location "/api/v1/orders/13"; respond `{"id":13,"customer_id":1,"status":"new"}` 201. Captured methods.txt: "POST   /api/v1/orders    -> 201", "HTTP/1.1 201 Created", "Location: /api/v1/orders/13".

Caddyfile@stage-0 L18-21: @getOrder = method GET, path /api/v1/orders/1; L41-43: respond `{"id":1,"customer_id":1,"status":"paid"}` 200. methods.txt: "GET    /api/v1/orders/1  -> 200" and the same body printed twice.

Caddy respond page (WebFetch summary): "Writes a hard-coded/static response to the client."; <status> "the HTTP status code to write"; <body> "the response body to write". Quoted bodies contain no {placeholders}; methods.txt prints the GET body verbatim twice.

methods.sh@stage-0: curl -sS -D - -o /dev/null -X POST ... "$base" | grep -Ei '^(HTTP/|Location:)'. Captured output: "Location: /api/v1/orders/13". Value is a constant at Caddyfile L38, so a second run prints the same line. scripts/up.sh exists at stage-0 (docker compose up -d --build --wait).

servers/index.md: "An ASP.NET Core app runs with an in-process HTTP server implementation." when-to-use-a-reverse-proxy.md: "When Kestrel is configured to listen on a port, Kestrel handles all traffic for that port"; a reverse proxy "Simplifies load balancing". Distribution across machines is outside Kestrel.

Local run 2026-09-27 (round 2): Python socket server on 127.0.0.1:9078 accepts, recv()s the request bytes, closes without writing; `curl -sS http://127.0.0.1:9078/` printed "curl: (52) Empty reply from server", exit=52.

issues.text: Unlisted claim (carried from round 1, still not in ledger): what the Caddy `header` directive does. Statement is correct: Caddy header page (WebFetch): "Manipulates HTTP response header fields." Kept minor: visible in the quoted block and verified.
issues.fix: Add a claim to .meta.json: {text: "In the stage-0 Caddyfile, the `header` lines set response headers (Content-Type, Location).", kind: "syntax", version_key: "caddy", section: 5, source_hint: "Caddy docs, header directive"}. No lesson text change.

issues.quote: You notice this when a program you wrote yourself that only reads the bytes off the connection and then closes it without writing anything back makes curl (the command-line program that sends a request and prints the reply) report "Empty reply from server"
issues.text: The claim is that parsing is Kestrel's special work, but the evidence shows a program that writes nothing back. I read it as "the special part is writing a reply", not "the special part is parsing". The link between the claim and the symptom is missing. The sentence is also long enough that I had to read it twice.
issues.fix: Split it into two sentences. Add a clause saying the empty reply happens because the program never produced a well-formed response, which is the second half of the parsing work named in the correction.

issues.quote: "Kestrel spreads requests across several machines for you."
issues.text: With only this lesson and my known list, I would not have thought of this. Nothing so far mentions several machines sharing requests, so the misconception feels like it comes from outside the lesson. It is easy to reject, though, and the correction uses only words I know.
issues.fix: Keep it if the outline requires it. Otherwise, swap it for a belief this reader could hold after section 2, e.g. "Caddy and Kestrel are the same kind of thing, so Kestrel also answers from a fixed file".

issues.quote: `handle @postOrder` is the part Caddy uses for a POST to `/api/v1/orders`, a name defined a few lines earlier in `Caddyfile`;
issues.text: The lines that define `@postOrder` are not in the quoted block, so I have to take on trust that this name means "POST to /api/v1/orders". I can still follow, because the prose tells me what it means.
issues.fix: Add "(not shown here)" after "a few lines earlier in `Caddyfile`" so the reader stops looking for the definition in the block.

issues.text: The lesson does not say what `methods.sh` sends or that its output includes a `Location` line. Step 2 implies it, so I can do the task, but at first I did not know what to look for in the output.
issues.fix: Add one short clause to step 1: "(it sends a GET and a POST to the lab and prints the status line and `Location` header of each)".

issues.quote: 5. Serving HTTP the way Kestrel does is deliberate, non-trivial parsing work, not an automatic side effect of listening on a port.
issues.text: "Non-trivial" is a little more than the lesson shows. The lesson says parsing is Kestrel's job but never shows why it is hard. This is not a new idea, just a stronger word than the lesson earned.
issues.fix: Drop "non-trivial", or replace it with the words section 6 uses: "is parsing work Kestrel exists to do, not an automatic side effect of listening on a port".
